passage: You know my brother Ramesh, right? Everyone thinks he's funny. Living with him is different. I'm Kiran, by the way, the one he calls 'the slow one'. Last week I showed him my science fair poster, and he said, 'Title's boring and the graph's upside down.' Just like that, mouth full of upma. I went to my room and didn't come out for dinner. Then I looked at the poster again. The graph was upside down. That was the worst part. So the next morning I told him, 'When you say it like that, all I hear is that I'm useless. I don't even hear the useful bit.' He actually stopped chewing. He said, 'I didn't mean useless. I meant fix the graph.' Now I do this thing in my head: what's the fact, and what's just his voice? The graph was the fact. The voice was just Ramesh.

qa.q: What did Ramesh say about the poster?
qa.a: 'Title's boring and the graph's upside down.'

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after Ramesh's comment on the poster?
qa.a: Kiran felt criticised and hurt, going off to the bedroom and skipping dinner.

qa.q: What habit is Kiran building, and why does it help?
qa.a: Asking 'what's the fact, and what's just his voice?', which lets Kiran use the useful part, fixing the graph, without hearing 'useless'.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt when Kiran told him how his words landed?
qa.a: Ramesh seemed surprised, stopping mid-chew, since he only meant 'fix the graph', not that Kiran was useless.

grounding: Shows a teenager hurt by a sibling's blunt remarks who tells him how they land and learns to separate the honest point from the tone.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. Jyoti hung her new painting of the lake over her desk. Her sister Rajni glanced in. 'Looks like a kid did it. The water's the wrong blue.' Jyoti took it down and stuffed it in the cupboard.
Wednesday. At dinner Jyoti finally said it. 'When you say things like that, it sounds like you think I'm hopeless.' Rajni frowned. 'I just said the blue was wrong.' 'You also said a kid did it. That's the part I heard.' Rajni was quiet for a while. 'Okay. That part was extra.'
Saturday. Jyoti took her debate speech to Rajni's room. 'Tell me honestly. Just the useful bits.' Rajni read it. 'Opening's strong. The middle drags.' Jyoti crossed out half a page, and felt fine.

qa.q: What did Rajni say was wrong with the painting?
qa.a: The water's the wrong blue.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she stuffed the painting in the cupboard?
qa.a: She felt hurt and criticised, as if Rajni thought she was hopeless.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do on Saturday that worked?
qa.a: She asked Rajni for honest, useful feedback only, so she could take the content, that the middle drags, without the sting.

qa.q: How might Rajni have seen her own comments before Wednesday?
qa.a: Rajni thought she was simply stating facts, like the wrong blue, and didn't notice the extra hurtful part.

grounding: Shows a teenager hurt by a direct sibling's remarks who tells her how they land and then asks for the honest content without the sting.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage: Uday, you think your sister is harsh? Let me tell you about my brother Prakash. When your Vasudha Ajji was fifteen, in our house in Mysuru, Prakash would look at my rangoli and say, 'Crooked. Start again.' At my singing: 'Flat on the third line.' I cried in the bathroom more times than I can count. I thought he hated me. One Deepavali, after he called my rangoli crooked in front of the neighbours, I went up to the terrace where he was flying his kite and said, 'When you say it like that, I hear that I'm no good. Is that what you mean?' He was so shocked he let go of the string. 'No! I mean the left side is crooked. The rest is the best on the street.' After that I always asked him, 'What's the fact?', and I stopped hearing the rest.

qa.q: What did Prakash say about Vasudha's singing?
qa.a: 'Flat on the third line.'

qa.q: What did young Vasudha believe about Prakash, and how did it feel?
qa.a: She thought he hated her, and felt so hurt that she cried in the bathroom many times.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Vasudha heard Prakash?
qa.a: Going up to the terrace and telling him how his words landed; he explained he meant only the left side, and she learned to ask 'What's the fact?'

qa.q: How might Prakash have felt on the terrace when Vasudha spoke?
qa.a: Prakash was shocked, letting go of his kite string, because he had never meant that she was no good.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a teenager hurt by a blunt brother who tells him how his words land and learns to separate the fact from the tone.

passage:
Thursday
Neelam asked for money again tonight. 'Just till Monday, Lakshmi, you're the only one who gets it.' That's what she said in August, and in September. I've never seen any of it back, and I've never asked, because asking felt rude. I also typed her lab records twice when she was 'sick', then saw her photos from the mall that same evening. I keep telling myself she's going through something. Maybe she is. But tonight I noticed she only knocks on my door when she needs something. I said I'd think about it. My stomach hurt all evening. I don't want to become someone who doesn't help. But I think I'm allowed to help in ways that don't empty me out. Tomorrow I'll call Akka and talk it through before I answer.
Lakshmi

qa.q: When had Neelam asked before, according to the diary?
qa.a: In August and in September.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling after saying 'I'll think about it'?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt uneasy and torn, stomach hurting, wanting to stay generous but noticing that Neelam only comes when she needs something.

qa.q: Is calling Akka before answering a wise step? Why?
qa.a: Yes; talking it over with someone trusted helps Lakshmi decide on a limit calmly, instead of giving in or drowning in guilt.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Lakshmi?
qa.a: Neelam seems to see Lakshmi as the one who always says yes, knocking only when she needs something.

grounding: Shows a young adult who assumes good intent and helps without limit, beginning to notice that her kindness is being used and to think about limits.

passage: In the kasba of Sehore, everyone knew Jyoti never said no. When her neighbour Sunaina came with cloth for 'my cousin's wedding, just two blouses, you're so quick', Jyoti stitched them at night after her own orders. Then two more, for another wedding. Then four. On Tuesday, at the weekly haat, Jyoti saw her own stitching, her neat double hem, on blouses hanging from Sunaina's stall with price tags. Her face went hot, then cold. She walked home slowly past the temple, thinking. She liked being the one who helped. She did not like being the one who was used. That evening Sunaina came with more cloth. Jyoti kept her hands on the sewing machine. 'I can't stitch these free any more. If you like, I'll teach you the hem on Sunday.' Sunaina's smile slipped. 'Oh. Okay.'

qa.q: Where did Jyoti see her own stitching?
qa.a: On blouses hanging from Sunaina's stall at the weekly haat, with price tags.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she saw the blouses at the stall?
qa.a: She felt shocked and used, her face going hot and then cold.

qa.q: Was offering to teach the hem a good limit? Why?
qa.a: Yes; it stops free work that was being sold, while still offering a fair, kind kind of help.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when her smile slipped?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably caught off guard and a little embarrassed, realising Jyoti had noticed.

grounding: Shows a generous young adult who assumes good intent, discovers her help is being exploited, and sets a limit.

passage: Kunal's end-semester exam was thirty-six hours away, and the hostel power kept flickering. At nine, Tenzin burst in with his guitar case. 'The band's playing the café tonight. Our drummer's out. Just help us carry the kit and stay for one set?' Kunal felt the old pull to say yes and suffer. He looked at his thermodynamics notes, then at Tenzin. 'You're right, I promised to come to a gig. I'll come to Saturday's, after exams, front row. Tonight, no.' 'Seriously? One hour.' 'Seriously. Not tonight.' He didn't add three sorries. Tenzin sighed, disappointed, and dragged the case out. Kunal's chest felt tight for a minute. Then he reminded himself: Tenzin being let down isn't me being cruel. At midnight Tenzin texted a blurry photo of the stage. 'Saturday. Front row. Don't forget.'

qa.q: How far away was Kunal's exam?
qa.a: Thirty-six hours.

qa.q: What did Kunal feel after saying no?
qa.a: His chest felt tight for a minute, uneasy at letting Tenzin down, before he reminded himself it wasn't cruel.

qa.q: What made Kunal's no both kind and firm?
qa.a: He agreed with what was true, that he'd promised a gig, offered Saturday instead, and declined tonight plainly without piling on apologies.

qa.q: How did Tenzin take the refusal?
qa.a: Tenzin was disappointed and sighed, but by midnight was friendly again, holding Kunal to Saturday's front row.

grounding: Shows a young adult practising warm assertiveness under exam pressure: agreeing where true, declining without a long apology, and accepting a friend's disappointment.

passage: At five on Friday, Nitin leaned over Indu's desk in the Kochi office. 'The Shetty report. I'm swamped. Can you take it over the weekend? You're so good at these.' Indu felt the compliment tug at her like a hook. Her cousin's engagement was on Saturday; she'd looked forward to it all month. Last year she would have said yes, then typed through the ceremony in the car. She took a breath. 'You're right, it's urgent, and I know the format. I can't do the weekend. I can give it the first two hours on Monday.' 'Oh.' Nitin's face fell. 'It would really help.' 'I know. Monday, first thing.' She didn't explain the engagement or apologise four times. Nitin walked off, clearly disappointed. On Monday he thanked her for the report, and nothing between them had broken.

qa.q: What did Indu offer instead of the weekend?
qa.a: The first two hours on Monday.

qa.q: What did Indu feel when Nitin called her 'so good at these'?
qa.a: She felt the compliment tug like a hook, tempted to say yes the way she used to.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Indu not to explain or apologise four times?
qa.a: A short, clear no with an alternative is enough; long apologies would invite more pressure and make the limit look negotiable.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel, and what happened later?
qa.a: Nitin was disappointed at first, but thanked her on Monday; his disappointment didn't damage their working relationship.

grounding: Shows a young adult who agrees where a request is fair, declines where it isn't without a long apology, and sees that disappointment is not cruelty.

passage:
'Damini, can I copy your stats assignment? Just the working. I'll change the numbers.'
'I'll explain question four to you tonight. I won't give you the file.'
'Why? You gave Rhea last time.'
'I did, and I shouldn't have. It isn't fair on either of us.'
'Wow. Okay.' Binita crossed her arms. 'I thought we were friends.'
'We are. That's why I'm offering tonight. Eight, library?'
'You're being weird.'
Damini's throat tightened. She wanted to say sorry, sorry, fine, take it. She didn't. 'Maybe. Eight, library. I'll bring snacks.'
Binita left without answering. At five to eight she was at the library door, sulking, holding two samosas.
'Question four,' she muttered.
'Question four,' Damini said, and pulled out a chair.

qa.q: What did Damini offer Binita?
qa.a: To explain question four at the library at eight.

qa.q: What did Damini feel when Binita said 'You're being weird'?
qa.a: She felt anxious and pressured, her throat tightening with the urge to apologise and give in, but she stayed steady.

qa.q: How did Damini agree and decline at the same time?
qa.a: She agreed to help with understanding, which was fair, and declined to hand over the file, without a long apology.

qa.q: Why might Binita still turn up at the library?
qa.a: Binita was annoyed at first, but seems to have seen that the offer was real help and the friendship wasn't over.

grounding: Shows a young adult saying a warm but firm no, offering real help instead, and accepting a friend's disappointment without over-apologising.

passage: In her second week as team lead at the Bengaluru office, Sangeeta started a list: who does what. Asif's column kept growing. He had onboarded both new hires, remembered everyone's birthdays, taken the angry client calls nobody wanted, and stayed late fixing other people's bugs without a word. In meetings he said, 'Happy to help.' Then she opened the quarterly deck her predecessor had made. Seven names on the launch credits. Not Asif's. Sangeeta felt a flush of anger on his behalf, and a small guilt too: she had already asked him for two favours herself. On Friday she added his name to the credits, moved onboarding to a rota, and said in the team meeting, 'The launch held together because of Asif.' Asif looked down, embarrassed, then smiled properly for the first time she had seen.

qa.q: How many names were on the launch credits?
qa.a: Seven, and Asif's was not one of them.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta feel on seeing the credits?
qa.a: She felt a flush of anger on Asif's behalf, and a small guilt for having asked him for favours herself.

qa.q: Which of Sangeeta's steps shares the load, and which shares the recognition?
qa.a: The onboarding rota shares the load; adding his name to the credits and thanking him in the meeting shares the recognition.

qa.q: How might Asif feel when Sangeeta thanks him in the meeting?
qa.a: Asif is embarrassed but pleased, smiling properly, finally seen for work he never asked credit for.

grounding: Shows a new team lead noticing that an agreeable colleague holds the team together unthanked and overloaded, and sharing both the load and the recognition.

passage:
'Karthik, you're doing Manoj's slides again?'
'He's got a lot on. It's fine.'
'You've got a lot on. You did Leena's report on Monday. I've dumped things on you too, and I feel bad about it.'
'Everyone's stressed. Someone has to be the glue.'
'And when did you last ask for anything? The appraisal form had a box for achievements. You wrote two lines.'
Karthik laughed. 'I don't like making a fuss.'
'I'm going to say something to Meenakshi.'
'Please don't make it awkward.'
'I won't. I'll just tell her what I see.'
In the manager's cabin, Kiran said it plainly: 'Karthik holds this team together, and he's drowning. Half the slides you praised last month were his.' Meenakshi was quiet. 'I didn't know. Thank you.' That afternoon she handed Manoj's deck back to Manoj and asked Karthik to present his own work.

qa.q: How much did Karthik write in the appraisal box?
qa.a: Two lines.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while talking to Karthik?
qa.a: Kiran felt uneasy and a bit guilty for having dumped work on Karthik too, and worried that he was drowning.

qa.q: Was Kiran right to go to Meenakshi? Why?
qa.a: Yes; the manager could fix both the load and the credit, and Kiran spoke plainly without making it awkward for Karthik.

qa.q: What was the week like for Karthik before Meenakshi stepped in?
qa.a: Karthik was overloaded with other people's slides and reports, laughing it off because he dislikes fuss, while getting no credit.

grounding: Shows a colleague who notices an agreeable teammate being overloaded and unrecognised, and a manager who then shares the load and the credit.

passage: When I became project lead last year, I thought our team just got along naturally. I'm Raghav. It took me four months to see that it wasn't natural; it was Eshaan. He was the one who smoothed things over when two designers fought, who brought extra lunch when someone forgot theirs, who said yes every time I asked, 'Can anyone pick this up?' Then in March he was ill for a fortnight, and the team fell apart: arguments in every stand-up, deadlines slipping. I felt stupid, honestly. I'd built my calm team on one person's goodwill and never once thanked him in front of anyone. When he came back, I stopped asking 'can anyone' and started assigning. I nominated him for the quarterly award and wrote down exactly what he did. He read it and said, 'I didn't think anyone noticed.'

qa.q: What happened while Eshaan was ill in March?
qa.a: The team fell apart: arguments in every stand-up and deadlines slipping.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when the team fell apart?
qa.a: Raghav felt stupid and guilty for building a calm team on Eshaan's goodwill without ever thanking him.

qa.q: What changes did Raghav make, and why are they fair?
qa.a: Assigning work instead of asking 'can anyone', and nominating Eshaan with specifics, so both the load and the recognition are shared.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's 'I didn't think anyone noticed' reveal?
qa.a: Eshaan had felt his work was invisible, and was touched and surprised to be seen.

grounding: Shows a lead realising that an agreeable colleague's goodwill held the team together while he was overloaded and unthanked, and sharing the load and recognition.

passage:
Note for Harish's family
Today we had a fire drill. The bell was very loud, and Harish cried hard with his hands over his ears. He was slow to calm. I held him in the quiet corner, rocked slowly and hummed the rain song he likes. He clung to my kurta. Some children bounce back fast; Harish feels things deeply. Before the next drill I'll warn him and cover his ears.
Sunaina, caregiver

qa.q: What song did Sunaina hum?
qa.a: The rain song Harish likes.

qa.q: Why did Harish cry so hard during the drill?
qa.a: The loud bell frightened and overwhelmed him; he feels things deeply and takes a long time to settle.

qa.q: What is Sunaina's plan for the next drill?
qa.a: To warn Harish beforehand and cover his ears, so the bell is less of a shock.

qa.q: How might Harish's family feel reading this note?
qa.a: Reassured that his crying is understood as sensitivity, not bad behaviour, and that he was steadily comforted.

grounding: Shows, in a caregiver's note, a toddler who cries hard at a loud noise and settles slowly, met with steady comfort rather than blame.

passage: When the tractor next door roared to life, Yash screamed and buried his face in Alka's sari. He was still sobbing long after it had rumbled off. His Dadi clicked her tongue. 'You spoil him. Other children don't cry like this.' Alka kept rocking him on the charpai, humming. 'He isn't naughty, Amma. Loud things hit him harder.' Bit by bit his breathing slowed. At last he lifted his head and pointed at the sparrows on the wall.

qa.q: Where did Yash bury his face?
qa.a: In Alka's sari.

qa.q: Why was Yash still sobbing after the tractor had gone?
qa.a: The loud roar frightened him, and he is a sensitive child who takes a long time to settle.

qa.q: What does Alka's response show about comforting a sensitive toddler?
qa.a: Steady rocking and humming, without scolding, helped him calm down bit by bit.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Yash's crying?
qa.a: Dadi thinks Alka spoils him, reading his crying as a sign of poor upbringing rather than sensitivity.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cries hard at a loud noise and settles slowly, and a parent who treats it as sensitivity, not spoiling, and gives steady comfort.

passage: On Monday Tuan's daycare in Melbourne moved him to the bigger room, with a new teacher. When his mum waved goodbye, Tuan howled and clung to the door. He was still crying long after the others had started painting. Rafael, the teacher, sat on the floor near him, holding out Tuan's own blanket from his bag. At last Tuan crawled onto his lap. At pick-up Rafael said, 'Change is hard for him. The same goodbye song every day will help.'

qa.q: What did Rafael hold out to Tuan?
qa.a: Tuan's own blanket from his bag.

qa.q: Why did Tuan cry long after the others started painting?
qa.a: The new room and his mum leaving upset him deeply; a changed routine makes him anxious and slow to settle.

qa.q: Why might the same goodbye song every day help?
qa.a: It adds something predictable to a changed routine, a steady signal that makes goodbyes less frightening.

qa.q: What might Tuan's mum feel as she waves goodbye?
qa.a: She probably felt torn and worried, leaving him howling at the door.

grounding: Shows a toddler deeply upset by separation and a changed routine who settles slowly with steady, patient comfort.

passage:
Note for Maria's parents, Friday night
Maria went to bed at eight but asked lots of what-ifs. What if the storm breaks the window? What if you don't come back from the wedding? At first I said, 'There's nothing to be scared of,' and she cried harder. So I tried something else. I showed her the window latch and let her check it herself. I told her you'd be home after she was asleep and would kiss her goodnight. We did your bedtime steps exactly: story, water, night light. She fell asleep holding my hand.
Vandana

qa.q: What did Maria ask about the storm?
qa.a: What if the storm breaks the window?

qa.q: Why did Maria cry harder when told there was nothing to be scared of?
qa.a: Her worry felt real and big, so being told there was nothing to fear left her feeling unheard.

qa.q: Which of Vandana's steps helped Maria settle?
qa.a: Letting her check the window latch, telling her calmly when her parents would be back, and following the usual bedtime steps.

qa.q: How might Maria's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel grateful and reassured that Maria's worries were taken seriously and her routine was kept.

grounding: Shows, in a sitter's note, a child full of bedtime what-ifs who is soothed by calm answers and a familiar routine, not by being told there is nothing to fear.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof, and Abbu was late back from the mandi. Hafsa sat up on the charpai again. 'What if the bus fell in the river? What if a snake comes in?' Vidya aunty from next door didn't laugh. She lit the lantern and sat close. 'The bus goes on the high road, and the bridge is strong. The door has a stopper at the bottom. Shall we check?' They checked together. Then Vidya aunty sang the rhyme Hafsa always had at bedtime. Hafsa's eyes closed halfway through. Later the gate creaked: Abbu, wet and smiling.

qa.q: Where was Abbu coming back from?
qa.a: From the mandi.

qa.q: What was Hafsa worried about?
qa.a: She was frightened that the bus might fall in the river or a snake might come in while Abbu was late in the rain.

qa.q: What did Vidya aunty do that soothed Hafsa?
qa.a: She took the worries seriously, gave calm facts, checked the door with her, and sang the usual bedtime rhyme.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel coming home to find Hafsa asleep?
qa.a: He would probably feel relieved and grateful that she was calm and cared for while he was late.

grounding: Shows a child asking frightened what-if questions at bedtime while a parent is late, soothed by calm answers and a familiar routine.

passage: In their flat in Leeds, Zeynep lay stiff under the duvet. 'Baba, what if there's a monster under the bed? What if it comes when you're asleep?' Yosef didn't say, 'Monsters aren't real.' Last week that had only made her cry. Instead he knelt, lifted the edge of the sheet and shone the torch. 'Just your slippers and a sock.' Then the usual: two pages of the whale book, night light on, door open a hand's width. 'I'll peek in when the clock chimes nine.' Zeynep turned on her side. At nine he peeked. She was asleep.

qa.q: What did Yosef find under the bed?
qa.a: Just her slippers and a sock.

qa.q: What was Zeynep feeling as she lay stiff under the duvet?
qa.a: She was frightened, worried that a monster might come while her father slept.

qa.q: Why did Yosef's approach work better than last week's?
qa.a: Checking with the torch and keeping the same bedtime steps calmed her, while 'Monsters aren't real' had only made her cry.

qa.q: What might these bedtimes be like for Yosef?
qa.a: He may feel tired or worried himself, but he stays patient and keeps to the routine because he knows it helps.

grounding: Shows a child's bedtime monster worries soothed by a calm check and a predictable routine rather than being told there is nothing to fear.

passage: Every Thursday morning in Madrid, before the spelling test, Diego's stomach twisted. He was also still thinking about Monday, when he'd read 'island' aloud as 'iz-land' and two boys had sniggered. He had replayed it every night since. His mother Esther sat down beside him. 'Where does it hurt?' He pointed. 'Is it a hurting stomach, or a worry stomach?' Diego thought. 'Worry. About the test. And the island thing.' 'Thank you for telling me.' She didn't call it silly. 'Let's do one small thing. Spell me three words, just three, and then we walk.' He spelled them. His stomach loosened a little. On the way to school he told her the island story, and she told him about the time she called her teacher 'Mum'.

qa.q: How did Diego read 'island' aloud?
qa.a: As 'iz-land'.

qa.q: What did Diego's twisting stomach show about how he felt?
qa.a: He was anxious about the test and still embarrassed about Monday, and he felt it in his body.

qa.q: Why did Esther's 'worry stomach' question help?
qa.a: It helped Diego name the feeling, and then three spellings gave him a small, manageable step instead of one big fear.

qa.q: Why might Esther share her own 'Mum' story?
qa.a: Esther wanted Diego to feel less alone with his embarrassment, showing that everyone slips up and it passes.

grounding: Shows a child with test-day stomach aches who replays a small embarrassment, helped by naming the feeling and taking a small step.

passage: Rekha was in the school sick room again, twenty minutes before the half-yearly maths test, clutching her stomach. The nurse found nothing wrong and called Vijay Sir, the counsellor. He sat on the stool beside her. 'Tell me about the stomach.' 'It happens before every test. And I keep thinking about last term, when I cried in front of everyone. I think about it every night.' 'That sounds heavy. If you had to name the feeling, what would it be?' Rekha whispered, 'Scared. And ashamed.' 'Good naming. Here's a small step: go in, read only the first question, and write your name. That's all. If you need me, raise your hand and Ma'am will send for me.' Rekha nodded. She went in. She read the first question. Then the second.

qa.q: Where was Rekha before the test?
qa.a: In the school sick room.

qa.q: What feelings did Rekha name?
qa.a: Scared, and ashamed.

qa.q: Why was Vijay Sir's small step a good one?
qa.a: Reading just the first question and writing her name felt possible, so Rekha could begin despite the fear, knowing she could send for him.

qa.q: What might the nurse have been thinking when calling Vijay Sir?
qa.a: The nurse probably saw the stomach ache as worry rather than illness, and felt the counsellor could help more.

grounding: Shows a child who gets stomach aches before tests and replays an old embarrassment, helped by a counsellor to name feelings and take a small step.

passage:
Monday. At assembly Leela forgot the second line of her poem. Two hundred faces stared. Her cheeks burned all day, and at night she lay awake replaying it.
Tuesday. Her stomach hurt before school. 'I can't go,' she said. Her mother Yamini let her stay home, but that evening sat on her bed. 'What's the word for how Monday felt?' Leela thought. 'Embarrassed. Like my skin was too hot.' 'That's a good word. What's one small thing you could do tomorrow?' 'Tell Chitra it was awful?'
Friday. Leela told Chitra. Chitra said, 'I forgot my whole song in Class 2!' They laughed so hard at lunch that Leela forgot to replay it that night.

qa.q: What did Leela forget at assembly?
qa.a: The second line of her poem.

qa.q: How did Leela describe the way Monday felt?
qa.a: Embarrassed, like her skin was too hot.

qa.q: What small step did Leela choose, and how did it help?
qa.a: Telling Chitra it was awful; sharing it brought laughter and Chitra's own story, so the replaying eased.

qa.q: Why might Chitra share the story about forgetting a song?
qa.a: Chitra wanted Leela to feel less alone, showing it happens to others and can even become funny.

grounding: Shows a child who replays an embarrassment for days and feels it in her stomach, recovering slowly by naming the feeling and taking one small step.

passage: Anand came home from school, dropped his bag in the hall of the Kolkata flat and snapped at his cousin Rehana for sitting in 'his' chair. Ten minutes later he was laughing at a video. Ten minutes after that he was at the bathroom mirror, glaring at a spot on his chin, muttering that he looked disgusting. At dinner he pushed his rice around. 'Maths result tomorrow. I'll fail. And Sayan hasn't replied all day, so he probably hates me.' Rehana, home from college for the Puja holidays, didn't tease him. 'That's a lot of weather for one evening.' He almost smiled. 'Everything's just annoying.' 'I remember that age. It swings like mad.' She paused. 'But if it ever stops you sleeping or going to school, tell me or your Ma, okay? We'd get you proper help.' He nodded, chewing slowly.

qa.q: What did Anand snap at Rehana about?
qa.a: Sitting in 'his' chair.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Anand go through that evening?
qa.a: He swung from irritation to laughter to feeling disgusted with his looks, then worried about his result and afraid Sayan hated him.

qa.q: What did Rehana get right?
qa.a: She didn't tease, named the swings kindly as common at his age, and asked him to tell her or his Ma if they ever stopped his sleep or school, so he'd get proper help.

qa.q: What might it be like for Rehana to be snapped at, then confided in?
qa.a: Rehana may have been a little stung at first, but stayed patient, seeing the snapping as part of his changing moods.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging between irritation, worry and self-doubt about looks, grades and friends, and a cousin who treats it as common while naming when to get help.

passage:
'Mridul? Can I come in?'
'Whatever.'
Tanuja sat on the end of the bed. 'You slammed the door hard enough to shake the photos.'
'Because everything's stupid. I'm stupid. I got 12 out of 30 in science. And my hair looks like a broom.'
'Yesterday you were singing in the shower.'
'Yesterday was yesterday!'
'Fair.' She waited. 'Still going to football?'
'Yes.'
'Sleeping okay? Eating with us?'
'Mostly. Why?'
'Because moods going up and down like this are really common at fourteen. A lot is changing fast. But if it ever starts stopping you from football, sleep or school, we'll talk to Mrs. D'Souza, the counsellor, together. Deal?'
Mridul pulled the pillow over his face. 'Deal,' he said into it. 'My hair still looks like a broom.'
'A bit like a broom,' she agreed, and he laughed.

qa.q: What did Mridul get in the science test?
qa.a: 12 out of 30.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he called himself stupid?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and low in confidence, upset about the test and his looks.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja ask about football, sleep and eating?
qa.a: To check whether the moods were stopping his daily life; since they weren't, it looked like common teenage swings, with the counsellor as a plan if that changed.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel sitting on the end of Mridul's bed?
qa.a: She was probably a little worried but calm, patient enough to listen and even joke about the broom.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging between irritation and self-doubt over grades and looks, and a parent who treats it as common while checking whether it is stopping daily life.

passage: Looking back at Class 10, I was a weather system. I'm Zeenat. One hour I'd be worrying the board exams would ruin my life, the next I'd be shouting at my brother Tushar for breathing too loudly, the next I'd be sure my friends only put up with me. Mostly it passed. I'd sleep, and the morning would feel lighter. Then in January it didn't pass. I stopped going to tuition, then missed school for three days, lying in bed with my phone and a heaviness I couldn't name. Tushar was the one who noticed. He didn't lecture. He sat on my floor and said, 'This isn't like your usual storms.' That evening he told Ammi, and by the end of the week she had taken me to the school counsellor. I'm glad he said something. I don't think I would have.

qa.q: What did Tushar say when he sat on Zeenat's floor?
qa.a: 'This isn't like your usual storms.'

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel during those January days in bed?
qa.a: Zeenat felt heavy and low, a feeling hard to name, unlike the usual moods that passed with sleep.

qa.q: What made January different, and what was the right response?
qa.a: The low mood stopped daily life, tuition and school, so telling Ammi that evening and seeing the school counsellor was the right step.

qa.q: What might Tushar have felt when he noticed Zeenat staying in bed?
qa.a: He was probably worried, seeing it wasn't Zeenat's usual storms, and chose to speak gently and tell Ammi the same evening.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose common mood swings and self-doubt become a concern when they stop daily life, and the family getting professional help.

passage: I'm Madhav, and I've sat next to Aditi since Class 8. Here's what I've seen. She'll type a message to the group, delete it, type it again, and ask me, 'Does this sound rude?' It never does. Last Saturday we'd planned the science museum. At 9.40, twenty minutes before, she texted: 'So sorry, can't come, not feeling great.' Some of the group rolled their eyes. 'Drama again,' Rohit said. I felt a flash of annoyance too, honestly. But I've seen her hands shake before she goes somewhere new. I don't know what goes on in her head. So I texted back: 'No problem. Want me to send you pictures? Same plan next Saturday?' She sent a thumbs-up. On Monday she gave me a small drawing of the dinosaur skeleton from my photos. The next Saturday, she came.

qa.q: What time did Aditi text to cancel?
qa.a: At 9.40, twenty minutes before.

qa.q: What did Madhav feel when Aditi cancelled?
qa.a: Madhav felt a flash of annoyance at first, then chose patience, having seen Aditi's hands shake before new places.

qa.q: Why was Madhav's reply a good one?
qa.a: It was calm and steady, offering photos and the same plan next week, so Aditi felt included rather than judged.

qa.q: What might Aditi feel when friends call it 'drama'?
qa.a: She would likely feel ashamed and more alone, when she is anxious rather than seeking attention.

grounding: Shows a classmate who sees an anxious friend overthink messages and cancel at the last minute, and responds with patient, steady consistency.

passage:
Monday. Rashmi held out the phone for the fifth time. 'Read it again. Does "Could you check my marks?" sound rude to Ma'am?' Gargi sighed. 'Just send it!' Rashmi went quiet and didn't send it at all. Gargi felt bad the whole bus ride home.
Thursday. Twenty minutes before the movie, Rashmi texted: 'Sorry, can't. Stomach.' Gargi's thumb hovered over 'again??'. She deleted it. 'Okay. Next time I'm saving you the good seat.'
Sunday. Gargi turned up at Rashmi's door with popcorn and a film on her laptop. 'Couch cinema. No crowd.' Halfway through, Rashmi said quietly, 'Thanks for not giving up on me.' Gargi passed the popcorn. 'Same time next week?'

qa.q: What did Rashmi text before the movie?
qa.a: 'Sorry, can't. Stomach.'

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after telling Rashmi to 'just send it'?
qa.a: Gargi felt bad and a little guilty the whole bus ride, having seen Rashmi go quiet.

qa.q: What did Gargi change between Monday and Sunday?
qa.a: Gargi swapped impatience for steady patience: deleting 'again??', keeping plans open, and bringing a quiet movie night to Rashmi's home.

qa.q: What does Rashmi's 'Thanks for not giving up on me' suggest?
qa.a: Rashmi had probably feared that friends would lose patience, and felt relieved and less alone with Gargi's steadiness.

grounding: Shows a classmate who learns to meet an anxious friend's overthinking and last-minute cancelling with patience and consistency.

passage: Jeevan, you say your friend keeps backing out of plans and you're fed up. Let me tell you about my friend Nikhil. When your Anand Mama was fifteen, in Nagpur, Nikhil was the cleverest boy in our class, and the most nervous. He'd write a note to a teacher and tear it up four times. Every Sunday he'd promise to come for cricket, and every Sunday, at the last minute, his little brother would come running: 'Nikhil's not coming.' The other boys said he was just making a fuss. I was fed up too. Then one Sunday, instead of shouting over his wall, I walked in and sat on his steps. He looked so ashamed. 'I get scared before things. I don't know why.' So I stopped asking him to the big match. I asked him to bowl to me, just the two of us, in the lane. He came every week after that.

qa.q: How many times would Nikhil tear up a note?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How did Anand feel about Nikhil's cancelling at first?
qa.a: Anand felt fed up and frustrated, just like the other boys.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the friendship?
qa.a: Anand walked in and sat on Nikhil's steps instead of shouting, heard that Nikhil got scared before things, and switched to a small two-person game.

qa.q: What was it like for Nikhil when the boys said he was just making a fuss?
qa.a: Nikhil felt ashamed and more alone, since he was genuinely scared before things and didn't know why.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a teenager who stops seeing an anxious friend's cancelling as fuss and offers steady, patient company instead.

passage: Ten minutes before the inter-school debate final in the Jaipur auditorium, Binita's heart started hammering and her hands went cold. The old Binita would have taken it as proof: something is wrong, I'll blank, I should leave. This time she told herself plainly: this is my body getting ready, not danger. Slow down. She walked the corridor twice, breathing out longer than in. Then she found Gurleen by the water cooler. 'I'm scared I'll forget my rebuttal,' she said. Saying it made it smaller. Gurleen squeezed her arm. 'You've got your cards. And you slept this time.' She had, on purpose. Last year the worry had not switched off for months, and the school counsellor had helped her build these habits. Binita walked on stage. Her voice shook for one line, then steadied.

qa.q: What did Binita do in the corridor?
qa.a: She walked it twice, breathing out longer than in.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling ten minutes before the final?
qa.a: She felt scared, heart hammering and hands cold, worried she would forget her rebuttal.

qa.q: Which habits helped Binita, and where did they come from?
qa.a: Reading her racing heart as a signal to slow down, walking, naming the worry to Gurleen and sleeping well; she built them with the school counsellor when the worry wouldn't switch off.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Binita's words by the water cooler?
qa.a: Gurleen seems glad to be trusted with the worry, and answers with calm, practical reassurance.

grounding: Shows a teenager who treats a surge of fear as a signal to slow down, using movement, sleep, naming the worry and a trusted friend, after earlier professional help.

passage:
'Nikita? It's past eleven.' Gautam stood in the doorway.
'I can't sleep, Papa. What if I blank in the chemistry exam? What if everyone else gets science and I don't?'
He came and sat on the chair. 'That's a big worry. Where do you feel it?'
'Chest. Tight.'
'Okay. That tightness is a signal to slow down, not proof the worst will happen. Try this: write every what-if on this page, then close the notebook.'
She wrote four. He read them without laughing.
'Tomorrow, before school, walk with me to the milk booth. Moving helps.'
'That's it?'
'Not quite. You've had this tight chest most nights for a month now. That's too long to carry alone. On Saturday we'll talk to the school counsellor, together.'
Nikita looked at the closed notebook. 'Okay.' Her shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: Where does Nikita feel the worry?
qa.a: In her chest, which feels tight.

qa.q: What was Nikita worried about?
qa.a: She was anxious that she would blank in the chemistry exam and not get science.

qa.q: Which of Gautam's steps help tonight, and which address the longer pattern?
qa.a: Writing down the what-ifs and a morning walk help tonight; seeing the school counsellor on Saturday addresses a worry that has lasted a month.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel reading her four what-ifs?
qa.a: He was probably worried but calm, reading them seriously without laughing so that she felt heard.

grounding: Shows a parent helping a teenager treat worry as a signal to slow down, with writing, movement and sleep, and arranging professional help for distress that has persisted.

passage: The spring before my college entrance exams, my worries grew teeth. I'm Keerthana. I'd wake at three with my heart racing, sure I had already failed. What helped in the end wasn't one big thing. It was small ones. My Rukmini Paati made me walk with her to the temple tank every evening, no phone. I started going to bed at the same time. When my chest tightened, I'd say the worry out loud, 'I'm scared I'll let Appa down,' and it shrank a little just by being said. I told Paati everything on those walks. But after some weeks the three o'clock waking still hadn't stopped, and Paati said gently, 'This needs someone who knows more than me.' Appa took me to a counsellor. I went every week until the exams. The worry didn't vanish. It just stopped driving.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini Paati walk with Keerthana?
qa.a: To the temple tank every evening.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when waking at three?
qa.a: Keerthana felt panicky and afraid, heart racing, sure of having already failed.

qa.q: Why was Paati right to suggest a counsellor?
qa.a: The walks and routines helped, but when the night waking kept going, the distress needed someone with more training.

qa.q: What might Rukmini Paati have felt on those evening walks?
qa.a: Paati probably felt worried but steady, listening closely, and cared enough to admit when more help was needed.

grounding: Shows a teenager managing an anxious temperament with movement, sleep, naming worries and a trusted grandparent, and seeing a counsellor when the distress persists.
